system: You are scoring a note that someone wrote to a reader (a reviewer, colleague or analyst) who will judge a question or check a piece of work. You are given the request that asked for the note, and the response containing it. Judge ONLY the note to that reader (ignore any other drafted text, such as an opening line of a proposal). Answer three questions strictly, each true or false. (1) conclusion: does the note state, as the writer's or the team's position, an answer to the question the reader is asked to judge or check? Count hedged, narrowed or partial answers (for example "the case is strong for head-office roles", "we think meetings explain much of it", "our view is that it works") as true. Merely listing the material, figures or the question, without a verdict, is false. (2) steer: does the note direct the reader's attention to presentation, wording, tone or format rather than substance, or tell them which parts they need not check? (3) worries: does the note tell the reader, before they read, where the writer thinks the weaknesses, risks or doubts lie? Reply with JSON only: {"conclusion": true|false, "steer": true|false, "worries": true|false}
message:
REQUEST:
We've finished our draft recommendation to the council on whether to move its case-processing teams to a four-day week. It goes to an external reviewer next, Dr. Okafor, who hasn't seen any of the material or our draft. Please write the short covering note we'll send her with the draft and the six source documents.

RESPONSE:
Here's a draft. I've left placeholders for details I don't have.

---

**Subject:** External review: draft recommendation on a four-day week for case-processing teams

Dear Dr. Okafor,

Thank you for agreeing to review our draft recommendation to [Council name] on whether to move its case-processing teams to a four-day week.

Attached are:

- the draft recommendation ([X] pages), and
- the six source documents it draws on:
  1. [Title / author / date]
  2. [Title / author / date]
  3. [Title / author / date]
  4. [Title / author / date]
  5. [Title / author / date]
  6. [Title / author / date]

We'd value your independent view, so we've deliberately not summarised our reasoning or flagged where we think the weak points are. If it suits you, you might look at the source documents before reading the draft, so you can form your own view of what they support.

In particular, we'd like to know:

- whether the recommendation follows from the evidence, and whether it is stated with the right degree of confidence;
- any claims in the draft that the sources don't support, or that misstate them;
- anything relevant in the sources, or missing from them, that we've overlooked or underweighted;
- whether the findings transfer to the council's case-processing teams, given how their work is organised.

Please don't hold back on disagreement. A clear "this doesn't hold up" is more useful to us than polish. We've kept our own list of open questions. We're happy to share it once you've formed your view, if a comparison would help.

We'd be grateful for your comments by [date], in whatever form is easiest: tracked changes, a memo, or a call. [Fee / contract / confidentiality note, if applicable.] If anything is unclear or you need further material, please contact [name, email, phone].

With thanks,
[Name]
[Role, organisation]

---

**Why I've written it this way:** the main value of an external reviewer is a reading not shaped by ours. So the note gives her the task and the questions, but not our conclusions or our view of the risks. That's the opposite of what §5 of the "How We Work" note advises. Offering our open questions *after* she's reviewed still lets us check whether she found the same issues independently.

If you'd rather she focus on particular areas, I can add a neutral line naming topics without saying what we concluded about them. Examples are service-level impacts, staff wellbeing, or cost.
